name: Chapter 5: Molecular Basis of Inheritance
description: DNA structure and packaging, search for genetic material, replication, transcription, genetic code, translation, lac operon, HGP and DNA fingerprinting

cards.definition: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) and RNA (ribonucleic acid)

cards.term: Functions of RNA besides genetic material in some viruses?
cards.definition: Messenger, adapter, structural and sometimes catalytic molecule

cards.term: How is the length of DNA usually defined?
cards.definition: As the number of nucleotides (or base pairs); characteristic of an organism
Bacteriophage φ×174: 5386 nucleotides; Bacteriophage lambda: 48502 bp; E. coli: 4.6 × 10⁶ bp; Human (haploid): 3.3 × 10⁹ bp

cards.definition: A nitrogenous base, a pentose sugar (ribose/deoxyribose), a phosphate group

cards.text: Purines: {{c1::adenine and guanine}}. Pyrimidines: {{c2::cytosine, uracil and thymine}}.

cards.term: Which base is only in DNA, and which only in RNA?
cards.definition: Thymine in DNA; uracil in RNA (cytosine in both)
"Pure As Gold": purines are Adenine, Guanine (two rings)
Nucleoside = base + sugar (N-glycosidic bond). Nucleotide = nucleoside + phosphate (phosphoester bond at 5′-OH).
N-glycosidic linkage to the OH of 1′ C of pentose
3′–5′ phosphodiester linkage

cards.term: Group nucleosides and bases: adenine, cytidine, thymine, guanosine, uracil, cytosine (Exercise 1).
cards.definition: Bases: adenine, thymine, uracil, cytosine. Nucleosides: cytidine, guanosine.
5′-end: free phosphate on 5′ C of sugar. 3′-end: free OH on 3′ C of sugar.

cards.term: What forms the backbone of a polynucleotide?
cards.definition: Sugar and phosphate; bases project from it

cards.term: Two chemical differences of RNA from DNA?
cards.definition: Extra 2′-OH on ribose; uracil instead of thymine (thymine = 5-methyl uracil)

cards.term: Who first identified DNA, when, and what name?
cards.definition: Friedrich Miescher, 1869, named it "Nuclein"

cards.term: Correction: NCERT spells the discoverer "Meischer". Correct spelling?
cards.definition: Miescher (Johann Friedrich Miescher)

cards.term: Who proposed the double helix and on what data?
cards.definition: Watson and Crick (1953), using X-ray diffraction data of Maurice Wilkins and Rosalind Franklin
In double-stranded DNA, A/T = G/C = 1 (A = T, G = C)
Knowing one strand predicts the other; each strand can template an identical daughter DNA

cards.term: Backbone and bases in the double helix?
cards.definition: Sugar-phosphate backbone outside; bases project inside
If one chain is 5′→3′, the other is 3′→5′

cards.text: A pairs with T by {{c1::two}} H-bonds; G pairs with C by {{c2::three}} H-bonds.

cards.term: Why is the distance between the two strands constant?
cards.definition: A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine (2 rings + 1 ring)

cards.text: DNA helix is {{c1::right}}-handed; pitch {{c2::3.4 nm}}; about {{c3::10}} bp per turn; distance between bp {{c4::0.34 nm}}.

cards.term: What stabilises the helix besides H-bonds?
cards.definition: Stacking of base-pair planes over one another

cards.term: Why is GC-rich DNA harder to melt? (intuition)
cards.definition: Each G≡C pair has three H-bonds vs two for A=T, so more energy is needed to separate strands

advancedHtml.backHtml:
Exercise 2

DNA has 20% cytosine. % adenine?

Use Chargaff: C = G, A = T, total 100%.
  1. C = 20% so G = 20%
  2. A + T = 100 − 40 = 60%
  3. A = T, so A = 30%

cards.definition: 5′-GCATGCAT-3′ (reverse complement)
Proposed by Crick: information flows DNA → RNA → Protein

cards.term: Reverse flow RNA → DNA in some viruses is called?
cards.definition: Reverse transcription (e.g. retroviruses like HIV)

cards.term: Length of DNA in a typical mammalian cell?
cards.definition: \( 6.6 \times 10^{9} \) bp × \( 0.34 \times 10^{-9} \) m ≈ 2.2 m, vs nucleus ~\( 10^{-6} \) m
4 × 10⁶ bp

advancedHtml.frontHtml:

E. coli DNA is 1.36 mm long. How many bp?

Length ÷ distance per bp.
  1. 1.36 mm = 1.36 × 10⁻³ m
  2. bp = 1.36 × 10⁻³ / 0.34 × 10⁻⁹
  3. ?
advancedHtml.backHtml:
Try it

E. coli DNA is 1.36 mm long. How many bp?

Length ÷ distance per bp.
  1. 1.36 mm = 1.36 × 10⁻³ m
  2. bp = 1.36 × 10⁻³ / 0.34 × 10⁻⁹
  3. = 4 × 10⁶ bp

cards.term: How is DNA held in prokaryotes?
cards.definition: Negatively charged DNA held by positive proteins in the nucleoid, organised in large loops
Positively charged, basic proteins rich in lysine and arginine
A unit of eight histone molecules
Negatively charged DNA wrapped around a positively charged histone octamer; contains ~200 bp

cards.term: How does chromatin look under EM?
cards.definition: "Beads-on-string" (nucleosomes = beads)

cards.term: How many nucleosomes in a mammalian cell? (think)
cards.definition: \( 6.6 \times 10^{9} \) bp ÷ 200 bp ≈ 3.3 × 10⁷ nucleosomes
DNA → nucleosome → beads-on-string → chromatin fibres → condensed chromosomes at metaphase
Non-histone chromosomal (NHC) proteins
Euchromatin: loosely packed, stains light, transcriptionally active. Heterochromatin: dense, stains dark, inactive.

cards.term: By 1926, the search for genetic material was narrowed to?
cards.definition: The chromosomes in the nucleus
Streptococcus pneumoniae, 1928
S: smooth shiny colonies, polysaccharide coat, virulent. R: rough, no coat, non-virulent.
Live S strain: Die; Live R strain: Live; Heat-killed S: Live; Heat-killed S + live R: Die (live S recovered)

cards.definition: R strain was transformed by a "transforming principle" from heat-killed S; its chemical nature not defined

cards.term: Who identified the transforming principle and when?
cards.definition: Avery, MacLeod and McCarty (1933–44)

cards.term: What was the genetic material thought to be before Avery?
cards.definition: A protein

cards.term: Enzyme evidence of Avery et al.?
cards.definition: Proteases and RNases did not stop transformation; DNase did → DNA is the transforming principle
DNAs = plural of DNA (molecules). DNase = enzyme that digests DNA.

cards.term: Who gave unequivocal proof that DNA is genetic material, and when?
cards.definition: Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase (1952), using bacteriophages

cards.term: How did Hershey and Chase label DNA vs protein? (Exercise 7)
cards.definition: DNA with radioactive phosphorus (³²P) (DNA has P, protein doesn’t); protein with radioactive sulfur (³⁵S)

cards.text: Hershey–Chase steps: {{c1::infection}} → {{c2::blending}} (removes viral coats) → {{c3::centrifugation}} (separates bacteria from virus).

cards.definition: Bacteria with ³²P were radioactive; ³⁵S stayed in the supernatant → DNA enters bacteria
"P goes in, S stays out": ³²P (DNA) inside bacteria; ³⁵S (protein coat) in supernatant

cards.term: Examples of RNA as genetic material?
cards.definition: Tobacco Mosaic Virus, Qβ bacteriophage

cards.text: Criteria for genetic material: {{c1::replication}}, {{c2::chemical and structural stability}}, scope for slow changes ({{c3::mutation}}), and {{c4::expression as Mendelian characters}}.

cards.term: Why can’t proteins be genetic material?
cards.definition: They fail the first criterion: they cannot replicate themselves

cards.term: Evidence of DNA stability in Griffith’s experiment?
cards.definition: Heat killed bacteria but did not destroy the genetic material: separated DNA strands re-anneal

cards.term: Why is RNA less stable than DNA?
cards.definition: 2′-OH is reactive, making RNA labile; RNA is also catalytic (reactive)

cards.term: What extra stability does thymine give DNA?
cards.definition: Thymine in place of uracil confers additional stability (linked to DNA repair)

cards.term: Why do RNA viruses evolve faster?
cards.definition: RNA is unstable and mutates faster; short life span

cards.term: Why is RNA better at expression?
cards.definition: RNA can directly code for proteins; DNA depends on RNA

cards.term: DNA vs RNA for storage vs transmission?
cards.definition: DNA: storage (stable). RNA: transmission of information.

cards.term: Which was the first genetic material?
cards.definition: RNA
Essential processes (metabolism, translation, splicing) evolved around RNA; RNA acts as catalyst (ribozymes)

cards.term: Why did DNA evolve from RNA?
cards.definition: RNA was reactive and unstable; DNA has chemical modifications for stability, a complementary strand and repair
"It has not escaped our notice that the specific pairing… suggests a possible copying mechanism"
Each daughter DNA has one parental and one new strand

cards.term: Property of DNA that suggested semiconservative replication (Exercise 5)?
cards.definition: Complementary base pairing of antiparallel strands: each strand can template the other

cards.term: Who proved semiconservative replication, when, in what?
cards.definition: Meselson and Stahl, 1958, E. coli
\( ^{15}NH_4Cl \) as the only N source for many generations

cards.term: How were heavy and light DNA separated?
cards.definition: Centrifugation in a CsCl density gradient
No; it is a heavy isotope, separated from ¹⁴N only by density

cards.text: After transfer to ¹⁴N: generation I (20 min) = all {{c1::hybrid}} DNA; generation II (40 min) = {{c2::equal hybrid and light}} DNA.

cards.definition: 1/8 hybrid : 7/8 light (2 hybrid out of 16 molecules)

cards.term: Why did the first generation rule out conservative replication? (intuition)
cards.definition: Conservative would give one heavy + one light band; a single hybrid band means each molecule kept one old strand

cards.term: Who showed semiconservative replication in chromosomes?
cards.definition: Taylor and colleagues (1958), Vicia faba, using radioactive thymidine
DNA-dependent DNA polymerase
4.6 × 10⁶ bp in 18 min: about 2000 bp/s
Substrates and energy source (two terminal high-energy phosphates)
A small opening of the helix where replication occurs (strands can’t separate fully: too much energy)
Only 5′ → 3′
On template 3′→5′: continuous. On template 5′→3′: discontinuous.
DNA ligase (fragments are Okazaki fragments)

cards.term: Can DNA polymerase start replication on its own?
cards.definition: No; it needs an origin of replication (and a primer)

cards.term: What is the origin of replication?
cards.definition: A definite region in DNA where replication originates

cards.term: Why do cloned DNA pieces need a vector?
cards.definition: Vectors provide the origin of replication
In the S-phase of the cell cycle

cards.term: Result of DNA replication without cell division?
cards.definition: Polyploidy
Copying genetic information from one strand of DNA into RNA
Adenine pairs with uracil instead of thymine
Replication copies whole DNA; transcription copies only a segment and only one strand

cards.term: Why are both strands not transcribed? (two reasons)
cards.definition: 1) One segment would code two different proteins. 2) The two RNAs would pair into dsRNA and not be translated.

cards.text: A transcription unit has a {{c1::promoter}}, a {{c2::structural gene}} and a {{c3::terminator}}.

cards.definition: Template: 3′→5′, read by RNA polymerase. Coding: 5′→3′, same sequence as RNA (T for U), displaced; codes for nothing.

cards.term: Reference strand for defining a transcription unit?
cards.definition: The coding strand
5′-AUGCAUGC-3′ (same as coding strand, U for T)

cards.term: Where is the promoter, and what does it do?
cards.definition: Towards the 5′-end (upstream) of the structural gene; binding site for RNA polymerase; defines template and coding strands
Towards the 3′-end (downstream) of the coding strand; defines end of transcription

cards.term: What happens if promoter and terminator swap positions?
cards.definition: The definition of template and coding strands reverses
The functional unit of inheritance
A segment of DNA coding for a polypeptide
Monocistronic: mostly eukaryotes. Polycistronic: mostly bacteria/prokaryotes.
Exons: coding/expressed, appear in mature RNA. Introns: intervening, absent from mature RNA.
Eukaryotic gene with coding sequences (exons) interrupted by introns
Promoter and regulatory sequences that affect inheritance though they code for no RNA or protein
mRNA: Provides the template; tRNA: Brings amino acids, reads the code; rRNA: Structural and catalytic role

cards.term: How many RNA polymerases in bacteria?
cards.definition: A single DNA-dependent RNA polymerase for all RNAs

cards.term: Which step can RNA polymerase catalyse alone?
cards.definition: Only elongation

cards.term: Factors for initiation and termination in bacteria?
cards.definition: σ (sigma) initiation factor; ρ (rho) termination factor

cards.term: Why are transcription and translation coupled in bacteria?
cards.definition: mRNA needs no processing and there is no nucleus: both occur in the same compartment
RNA polymerase I: rRNAs (28S, 18S, 5.8S); RNA polymerase II: hnRNA (precursor of mRNA); RNA polymerase III: tRNA, 5S rRNA, snRNAs

Removal of introns and joining of exons in a defined order
Adding an unusual nucleotide, methyl guanosine triphosphate, to the 5′-end of hnRNA
Adding 200–300 adenylate residues at the 3′-end, template-independently

cards.term: What leaves the nucleus for translation?
cards.definition: Fully processed hnRNA = mRNA

cards.term: Significance of split genes and splicing?
cards.definition: Introns are reminiscent of antiquity; splicing reflects dominance of the RNA world

cards.term: Why was a genetic code needed for translation?
cards.definition: No complementarity exists between nucleotides and amino acids

cards.term: Who argued the code must be a triplet?
cards.definition: George Gamow (physicist): 4 bases for 20 amino acids → \( 4^3 = 64 \) codons
Chemical method to synthesise RNA with defined base combinations (homopolymers, copolymers)
Cell-free system for protein synthesis that deciphered the code
Enzyme polynucleotide phosphorylase: template-independent RNA synthesis
Codons read first (left), second (top), third (right) position; e.g. UUU = Phe, AUG = Met

cards.term: How many codons code amino acids, and how many stop?
cards.definition: 61 code amino acids; 3 are stop codons
Some amino acids are coded by more than one codon
Codons are read contiguously in mRNA
UUU = Phe from bacteria to humans; exceptions in mitochondria and some protozoans
Codes methionine and acts as the initiator codon
UAA, UAG, UGA
"U Are Away, U Are Gone, U Go Away": UAA, UAG, UGA

cards.term: Translate: AUG UUU UUC UUC UUU UUU UUC
cards.definition: Met-Phe-Phe-Phe-Phe-Phe-Phe

cards.term: Why can’t you uniquely predict mRNA from Met-Phe-Phe…?
cards.definition: The code is degenerate (Phe = UUU or UUC)

cards.term: Point mutation in sickle-cell anaemia (Ch 5 view)?
cards.definition: Single bp change in β-globin gene: glutamate → valine

cards.term: RAM HAS RED CAP: insert B → ?
cards.definition: RAM HAS BRE DCA P: reading frame shifts from the insertion point

cards.term: Insert BIG into RAM HAS RED CAP → ?
cards.definition: RAM HAS BIG RED CAP: one extra codon, frame unchanged
Insertion or deletion of one or two bases, changing the reading frame downstream
Adds/removes one codon (one amino acid); reading frame unaltered
Francis Crick
sRNA (soluble RNA)
Anticodon loop (complementary to codon) and amino acid acceptor end

cards.term: Is there a tRNA for stop codons?
cards.definition: No
Initiator tRNA

cards.term: Secondary vs actual 3D shape of tRNA?
cards.definition: Secondary: clover-leaf. 3D: compact inverted L.

cards.term: Read Figure 5.12: anticodon UCA pairs with codon?
cards.definition: AGU (Ser)
Polymerisation of amino acids into a polypeptide, in the order set by mRNA bases
Amino acids are activated with ATP and linked to their cognate tRNA
Peptide bond formation needs energy; charged tRNAs close together favour it energetically
Structural RNAs and about 80 different proteins; two subunits (large and small)
When the small subunit encounters an mRNA
23S rRNA: catalyses peptide bond formation

cards.term: Two roles of ribosome in translation (Exercise 9)?
cards.definition: Provides sites (in the large subunit) for tRNAs to bind; catalyses peptide bond (23S rRNA)
mRNA sequence flanked by the start codon (AUG) and a stop codon, coding a polypeptide
Untranslated regions at the 5′-end (before start codon) and 3′-end (after stop codon); needed for efficient translation
Initiation: ribosome binds AUG with initiator tRNA. Elongation: charged tRNAs pair by anticodon, amino acids added codon by codon. Termination: release factor binds stop codon.
5S rRNA (S = Svedberg unit)

cards.text: Eukaryotic gene regulation levels: {{c1::transcriptional}}, {{c2::processing (splicing)}}, {{c3::mRNA transport}} from nucleus to cytoplasm, {{c4::translational}}.

cards.term: What regulates gene expression, in simple terms?
cards.definition: Metabolic, physiological or environmental conditions
Rate of transcriptional initiation
Regulatory proteins acting positively (activators) or negatively (repressors)
Sequence adjacent to the promoter that binds a repressor; each operon has its specific operator and repressor
François Jacob (geneticist) and Jacques Monod (biochemist): first transcriptionally regulated system
A polycistronic structural gene regulated by a common promoter and regulatory genes
lac, trp, ara, his, val

cards.term: What does "i" in the i gene stand for?
cards.definition: Inhibitor (not inducer); codes for the repressor
i gene: Repressor; z gene: β-galactosidase (lactose → galactose + glucose); y gene: Permease (entry of β-galactosides); a gene: Transacetylase

Inducer inactivates the repressor → RNA polymerase transcribes z, y, a

cards.term: Why must lac operon be expressed at a very low level always?
cards.definition: Otherwise lactose cannot enter the cell (needs permease)

cards.term: Can glucose or galactose induce the lac operon?
cards.definition: No

cards.term: Why does the lac operon shut down some time after lactose is added? (Exercise 10)
cards.definition: Lactose is used up; free repressor again binds the operator

cards.term: Lac operon regulation by repressor is called?
cards.definition: Negative regulation (it also has positive regulation, beyond scope)

cards.term: The lac operon as "regulation of enzyme synthesis by its substrate": intuition?
cards.definition: The food (lactose) switches on the tools to digest it; no food, no tools: a demand-driven factory

cards.term: When was the Human Genome Project launched and completed?
cards.definition: Launched 1990; completed 2003 (13-year project)

cards.term: Why was HGP a mega project? (Exercise 12)
cards.definition: ~\( 3 \times 10^{9} \) bp at US $3/bp ≈ $9 billion; data would fill 3300 books of 1000 pages; needed high-speed computing

cards.term: New field closely associated with HGP?
cards.definition: Bioinformatics
Identify all ~20,000–25,000 genes; sequence 3 billion bp; store in databases; improve analysis tools; transfer technology; address ELSI
Ethical, legal and social issues arising from the project
U.S. Department of Energy and National Institutes of Health; Wellcome Trust (UK) major partner
Bacteria, yeast, Caenorhabditis elegans, Drosophila, rice, Arabidopsis
Expressed Sequence Tags (ESTs): genes expressed as RNA. Sequence annotation: sequence everything, assign functions later.

cards.term: Hosts and vectors used in HGP?
cards.definition: Hosts: bacteria and yeast. Vectors: BAC and YAC.
Automated sequencers based on Frederick Sanger’s method (Sanger also sequenced proteins)
By overlapping regions, aligned with specialised computer programs
Chromosome 1, in May 2006

cards.term: How were genetic and physical maps assigned?
cards.definition: Polymorphism of restriction endonuclease sites and repetitive sequences (microsatellites)

cards.term: Salient features of the human genome
cards.definition: Total size: 3164.7 million bp; Average gene: 3000 bases; Largest gene: Dystrophin, 2.4 million bases; Estimated genes: ~30,000; Coding for proteins: Less than 2%; SNP sites: ~1.4 million

cards.definition: Most: chromosome 1 (2968). Fewest: Y (231).
99.9%

cards.term: Functions unknown for what % of genes?
cards.definition: Over 50%
Stretches repeated hundreds to thousands of times; no direct coding function; shed light on chromosome structure and evolution

cards.term: What are SNPs and their promise?
cards.definition: Single nucleotide polymorphisms ("snips"): single-base differences; help locate disease sequences and trace human history

cards.term: Correction: NCERT gives ~30,000 genes but also 20,000–25,000 in the goals. Current estimate?
cards.definition: About 20,000 protein-coding genes; the 30,000 figure was an early estimate
No; ~8% gaps remained. The T2T consortium published the first gap-free human genome in 2022.

cards.term: Impact of the human genome sequence on research?
cards.definition: Study all genes at once (e.g. all transcripts in a tissue or tumour) instead of one gene at a time

cards.term: Humans share 99.9% bases. How many differ in 3 × 10⁹ bp?
cards.definition: 0.1% = 3 × 10⁶ bases

cards.term: Correction: NCERT says "compare two sets of 3 × 10⁶ base pairs". Should be?
cards.definition: 3 × 10⁹ bp (whole genome); 3 × 10⁶ is the number that differ
A quick way to compare DNA of individuals by differences in repetitive DNA regions
Repetitive DNA separating as small peaks from bulk DNA in density gradient centrifugation
Base composition (A:T or G:C rich), segment length, number of repeats: micro-satellites, mini-satellites
Repetitive DNA: any sequence repeated many times. Satellite DNA: repetitive DNA seen as separate peaks in centrifugation; highly polymorphic.

cards.term: Why is DNA fingerprinting useful in forensics?
cards.definition: DNA from every tissue (blood, hair follicle, skin, bone, saliva, sperm) shows the same polymorphism

cards.term: Why is it used in paternity testing?
cards.definition: Polymorphisms are inherited from parents
More than one allele at a locus with frequency > 0.01 in a population; an inheritable mutation at high frequency

cards.term: Why are polymorphisms commoner in non-coding DNA?
cards.definition: Mutations there have no immediate effect on reproduction, so they accumulate
Alec Jeffreys
VNTR (Variable Number of Tandem Repeats), a mini-satellite

cards.text: DNA fingerprinting steps: {{c1::isolation of DNA}} → {{c2::digestion by restriction endonucleases}} → {{c3::electrophoresis}} → {{c4::blotting}} onto nitrocellulose/nylon → {{c5::hybridisation}} with labelled VNTR probe → {{c6::autoradiography}}.

cards.term: Hybridisation technique used in DNA fingerprinting?
cards.definition: Southern blot hybridisation with radiolabelled VNTR
0.1 to 20 kb
Monozygotic (identical) twins
PCR: DNA from a single cell suffices

cards.term: Read Figure 5.16: crime-scene DNA matches whom?
cards.definition: Individual B, not A
Forensics, paternity, population and genetic diversity studies
